description_full: Eaton Corporation plc operates as a power management company in the United States, Canada, Latin America, Europe, and the Asia Pacific. It operates through Electrical Americas, Electrical Global, Aerospace, Vehicle, and eMobility segments. The company offers electrical and industrial components, power distribution and assemblies, residential products, single- and three-phase power quality and connectivity products, wiring devices, circuit protection products, utility power distribution products, and power reliability equipment; and hazardous duty electrical equipment, emergency lighting, fire detection, intrinsically safe explosion-proof instrumentation, and structural support systems. It also provides pumps, motors, hydraulic power units, hoses and fittings, and electro-hydraulic pumps; valves, cylinders, electronic controls, electromechanical actuators, sensors, aircraft flap and slat systems, and nose wheel steering systems; hose and thermoplastic tubing products, fittings, adapters, couplings, and sealing and ducting products; air-to-air refueling systems, fuel pumps, fuel inerting products, sensors, and adapters and regulators; oxygen generation systems, payload carriages, and thermal management products; wiring connectors and cables; and hydraulic and bag filters, strainers and cartridges, and golf grips for manufacturers of commercial and military aircraft, related aftermarket customers, and industrial applications. In addition, the company offers transmissions, clutches, hybrid power systems, superchargers, engine valves and valve actuation systems, locking and limited slip differentials, transmission controls, and fuel vapor components for the vehicle industry; and voltage inverters, converters, fuses, circuit protection units, vehicle controls, power distribution systems, fuel tank isolation valves, and commercial vehicle hybrid systems. The company was formerly known as Abeiron Limited. The company was founded in 1911 and is based in Dublin, Ireland.

financial_summary: Eaton Corporation, PLC is a large-cap industrials business with a $126.6B market cap on $27.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 10% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $3.6B in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.09× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 20× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 96% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Significant goodwill (38% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 9pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.61x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.7% of sector revenue and 1.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+9.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 12% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 21% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 32% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 1.09, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $910.2M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 45% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 68% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $167 (margin of safety -96%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 13%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $86.09 to $319 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 32.6 vs 23.1, EV/EBITDA 20.8 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 35.6 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 24% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 27 covering analysts target $466 on average, 43% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 9.6%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.21).
It converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.09x.
ROE of 21% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.9% of revenue on R&D and 0.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.3x net debt to EBITDA ($803.0M of cash against $8.8B of debt), with interest covered 20.5x.
Goodwill makes up 38% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.8% over 3 years and 9.0% over 5 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.07 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 56% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 49%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 3.3% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 22, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 88%.
Insider trading is two-way: 8 purchases and 4 sales over the past year, net $8.0M sold.
It returns 2.8% a year to shareholders (1.5% in buybacks and 1.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 53 consecutive years, raising it 6.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 97,303 employees, each generates about $282K of revenue, 0.8x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 4.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $37K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (8x revenue per employee).
